title: The overture of the prophet
introduction: Isaiah 1 introduces the whole book in miniature: a rebellious people, the Holy One they have despised, judgment on empty worship, and an invitation to cleansing. This class explores the characters, the covenant lawsuit, the prophet’s calling, and the meaning of holiness in public life.
finalWord: Isaiah 1 asks us to bring worship, trust, and conduct before the Holy One together. Read the chapter again, identify one place where it exposes false security, and pray for the grace to respond to its invitation. Teaching adapted from the supplied pastoral presentations; all direct biblical quotations above use WEB.

points.title: One prophet and four kings
points.text:
Isaiah son of Amoz speaks concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The four names give the ministry a setting that stretches across changing political conditions. Each reign also helps the class explore a recurring question: will Judah trust God, or rely on its own power?

Uzziah’s strength and prosperity turned into presumption. His attempt to take the priestly role in 2 Chronicles 26 ends in judgment and isolation. The year of his death frames Isaiah’s vision in chapter 6: an earthly king dies while the true King remains enthroned.

Jotham did what was right, yet the people continued to act corruptly. His reign warns us that a respectable surface and good leadership in one person do not automatically produce a faithful community.

Ahaz embodies fear and false trust. Under political pressure, he turns to Assyria, takes from the temple to pay tribute, and embraces corrupt worship. He contrasts with the call to trust God in Isaiah 7.

Hezekiah reforms worship and seeks God during the Assyrian crisis. Jerusalem’s deliverance offers a real note of hope. Yet his display before Babylon’s envoys in chapter 39 warns that success can expose another form of pride.

Discuss: What forms of confidence appear across these reigns? Where do crisis and prosperity test us differently?
points.alt: A muted burgundy engraving of Jerusalem beneath radiant light, an empty royal seat, and a living shoot growing from a stump.

points.title: The covenant lawsuit
points.text:
The opening summons heaven and earth as witnesses. This opening can be read as a covenant lawsuit, often called a rîb. Yahweh brings the case and judges it. Judah is addressed as the children he nourished, who have rebelled against him. The language recalls the covenant witnesses in Deuteronomy.

Hear, heavens, and listen, earth; for Yahweh has spoken: “I have nourished and brought up children and they have rebelled against me.
— Isaiah 1:2 (WEB)

The comparison with an ox and a donkey makes the charge painfully direct: even animals recognize the one who feeds them, while God’s people fail to understand. The wounded body and devastated land show the cost of this rebellion. Yet the small remnant in verse 9 already points to preserving mercy.

The courtroom setting also helps us hear the invitation in verse 18. God does not abandon the question of justice when he offers cleansing. He addresses the guilty people and calls them to respond.

Discuss: What does the family language add to the legal charge? How does verse 9 prepare us for the invitation that follows?

points.title: A messenger of the higher court
points.text:
Isaiah’s encounters with rulers show familiarity with the world of the court. This offers a lens for reading his calling: he speaks to Judah’s kings from the authority of the true King. A royal family connection is a later tradition; the biblical narrative does not give a complete account of his social background.

Thrones, robes, glory, and David’s house form part of the vocabulary of Isaiah’s royal hope. Watching human rulers fail makes the longing for righteous rule especially vivid. This is offered as a theological reading of the book, rather than a proven explanation of how every prophecy arose.

There is also a striking contrast within that hope. The book that announces an exalted ruler also describes the Servant who is despised and rejected. The courtly imagery does not erase the suffering through which the Servant’s mission is fulfilled.

Isaiah himself first confesses his unclean lips. His commission begins with cleansing, so he ministers as someone who has received mercy alongside the people he addresses.

Discuss: How does the vision of God’s throne challenge our understanding of human authority? What posture should receiving mercy produce in a teacher or leader?

points.title: Holiness reaches every sphere of life
points.text:
The Holy One of Israel is the one the nation has despised. Holiness explains why worship and injustice cannot be treated as unrelated matters. The sacrifices, assemblies, and prayers of verses 11–15 do not conceal hands full of blood.

Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Defend the fatherless. Plead for the widow.”
— Isaiah 1:17 (WEB)

The following comparison of four prophets offers a teaching framework. Hosea draws attention to home, marriage, and covenant love; Amos to the field, the market, and exploitation; Micah to neighbors, local justice, and leaders; Isaiah to the court, the temple, and national trust. None of these prophets is confined to one sphere.

Holiness was meant to shape the whole community. The temple could not remain a healthy center while injustice spread through the rest of life. Isaiah’s call to defend the fatherless and plead for the widow makes worship concrete.

Discuss: Which part of our life is easiest to keep separate from worship? What would seeking justice look like there this week?

points.title: Scarlet, snow, and the tree that withers
points.text:
The chapter holds an invitation and a warning together. God offers cleansing, calls for a willing response, exposes corrupt leadership, and promises to refine the city.

“Come now, and let’s reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they are red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
— Isaiah 1:18 (WEB)

Zion shall be redeemed with justice, and her converts with righteousness.
— Isaiah 1:27 (WEB)

The closing oaks and gardens belong to the exposure of misplaced worship. The people become like a withering oak and a garden without water. The teaching traces this reversal through the book: proud trees are brought down, and people who trust lifeless idols reflect their helplessness.

The later stump and shoot imagery in chapters 6 and 11 opens a hope that judgment does not exhaust. In the Christian reading developed in the class, the shoot from Jesse brings the promise of righteous rule into focus in Christ.

The presentation also mentions the later tradition that Isaiah was sawn apart under Manasseh. Hebrews 11:37 refers to such suffering without naming him, so this remains a tradition rather than a detail established by that verse.

Discuss: Where is the chapter calling for a change of direction? How do its promises encourage repentance without weakening the warning?
